The reported proportions themselves also warrant caution: if Z-scores were approximately normal, 79.9% below −2 and 3.8% below −3 for WHZ imply a mean near −2.3 and an SD of about 0.4, and the HAZ proportions imply a mean near −3.1 and an SD of about 0.7. These are narrower than the spread of about 1 usually seen in survey data, and may indicate measurement or data-handling problems, although a highly selected clinic population could also have a narrower distribution.Two further observations apply. First, wasting by WHZ (79.9%) was twice as frequent as acute malnutrition by MUAC (39.1%). The indicators identify overlapping but non-identical children, so some discordance is expected, but a gap of this size needs reconciliation with repeat measurements, which were not collected. Second, the direction of possible errors matters. An error in length or height shifts HAZ and WHZ in opposite directions, so one systematic length error cannot inflate stunting and wasting together. Underestimated weight (for example from scale zeroing or clothing) would raise wasting but not stunting, and overestimated age would raise stunting but not wasting. Very high prevalence of both therefore implies a genuinely vulnerable group, more than one independent source of error, or a computational or coding problem; the present data cannot distinguish among these.4.3.Comparison with other studiesFacility-based studies share the health-seeking selection of our cohort and are better comparators than population surveys, yet their estimates vary widely (Table 3). Stunting ranged from 14.4% in a Nepalese paediatric outpatient department (13) to 68.2% in the nearby Afgoi preprint (8), and reviews of paediatric hospital populations report undernutrition from 2.5 to 51% depending on population and definitions (14). This heterogeneity reflects referral role, whether a facility runs a nutrition programme that concentrates malnourished children, inclusion of sick or admitted children, underlying community burden, season and methods. Clinic-derived prevalence can diverge substantially from community prevalence and should not be used as a proxy for it (15). Our estimates lie above the range of the comparators in Table 3, including the Afgoi preprint, which was conducted in the same period; the two reports are complementary facility observations rather than independent district estimates.4.4.Possible explanations (hypotheses)The data cannot test the following explanations. Selection: caregivers who attend growth monitoring may do so because of concern about growth or illness, and recruitment from the attendance register would then enrol a more malnourished subgroup. Season: data were collected in the Jilaal dry season, when food and water scarcity and infection risk may be higher (7); we cannot say whether this is a seasonal peak. Displacement: displaced children may be over-represented among attendees and are widely reported to face compounded nutritional risk, but displacement status was not recorded, so this can be neither supported nor excluded. A community-based study of children in IDP camps in Hargeisa, Somaliland, reported 21.1% stunting (16); although design, age range and setting differ, it indicates that displacement does not by itself imply prevalence of the magnitude seen here.4.5.Feeding and morbidityReported prior exclusive breastfeeding (20.6%) is lower than the 33.7% reported for infants under six months in the 2020 national survey (3), but the indicators are not equivalent because ours is a retrospective report across all ages. Low colostrum feeding, incomplete vaccination and frequent recent diarrhoea suggest considerable clinical vulnerability in this cohort. This cross-sectional descriptive study cannot show whether these characteristics are related to stunting or wasting.4.6.Strengths and limitationsStrengths include use of WHO standards and procedures, three complementary anthropometric indicators, confidence intervals, and transparent reporting of data-quality gaps. Limitations are as follows. Recruitment was consecutive and non-probabilistic at a single hospital over two months, which introduces selection bias and prevents generalization, and no screening log exists to characterize non-participants. Duplicate measurements and inter-observer standardization were not performed, so measurement error cannot be excluded. The source of age data, oedema status and enrolment in nutrition programmes were not documented, all of which affect Z-scores and case mix. Feeding and illness data are caregiver-reported and prone to recall bias. Displacement status was not recorded. The design is descriptive, and no analysis of determinants was undertaken.4.7.ImplicationsAt facility level, children identified with growth faltering or acute malnutrition need guideline-based assessment, treatment or referral, feeding counselling, immunization catch-up and evaluation of recurrent infection. These findings should not guide district planning, which needs representative, seasonally repeated surveillance with duplicate measurements, routine recording of displacement status, and samples powered for comparison between host-community and displaced children.
full_text_sections.conclusion: 5.ConclusionChildren attending Afgooye Hospital for growth monitoring in February–March 2025 had a very high burden of stunting (94.3%) and wasting (79.9%), with 39.1% acutely malnourished by MUAC, as recorded and not independently verified. These findings describe a single-facility, health-seeking cohort and do not represent Afgooye district. They support strengthened facility-based nutrition care and representative community surveillance across seasons that includes displacement status and quality-controlled anthropometry.

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to assess the prevalence of undernutrition among children aged 6–59 months attending Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, to inform public health interventions.
analysis.study_design_and_population: A facility-based cross-sectional study was conducted at Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, between February and March 2025, involving 422 children aged 6–59 months.
analysis.methods: The study used a single-proportion formula to calculate the sample size with 95% confidence, 5% absolute precision, and an expected prevalence of 50%. Data were collected via an interviewer-administered questionnaire, and caregiver reports were verified against vaccination cards and medical records.
analysis.main_results: Among the 422 children, 94.3% (95% CI 91.7–96.1) were stunted, 55.9% severely stunted, 79.9% (95% CI 75.8–83.4) were wasted by weight-for-height Z-score, and 39.1% (95% CI 34.6–43.8) had acute malnutrition by MUAC.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The findings suggest a high prevalence of undernutrition in this clinic cohort, which may indicate measurement or data-handling issues, or a highly selected population with limited variability in nutritional status.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The results highlight the urgent need for targeted nutrition interventions in Afgooye Hospital and provide baseline data for future studies on undernutrition in the region.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The non-probability sampling approach may over-represent children with growth or health concerns, limiting generalizability, and the confidence intervals assume independent sampling without accounting for selection bias or measurement error.

analysis.summary_en: This facility-based cross-sectional study conducted at Afgooye Hospital, Somalia, between February and March 2025, assessed undernutrition among 422 children aged 6–59 months. The study found that 94.3% were stunted, 55.9% severely stunted, 79.9% wasted by weight-for-height Z-score, and 39.1% had acute malnutrition by MUAC. These results are based on caregiver-reported data verified against medical records. The study acknowledges limitations, including potential selection bias due to non-probability sampling and the assumption of independent sampling in confidence intervals. The high prevalence of undernutrition underscores the need for targeted interventions in the region, though the findings may not be generalizable beyond the clinic setting.

title: From eminence to evidence to intelligence-based medicine: optimising artificial intelligence to disrupt dogma in emergency departments

source_records.title: From eminence to evidence to intelligence-based medicine: optimising artificial intelligence to disrupt dogma in emergency departments

priority_tier_reason: 补充性记录、预印本或证据完整度有限
full_text: AbstractThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, intelligence-based medicine. Driven by the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), this emerging era offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care within high-stakes environments like emergency departments. However, this paradigm shift simultaneously introduces a critical risk of modernised, digital dogma, manifesting as algorithmic paternalism. If AI systems are deployed without rigorous oversight, they threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics, trading the unquestioned authority of historical figures for the presumed infallibility of machines. To safeguard care in emergency departments, AI must not operate unchecked. Adapting existing Learning Health System frameworks offers a pragmatic solution to govern AI integration. By embedding these computational technologies within continuous, self-correcting clinical ecosystems, departments can enforce robust data hygiene and rigorously audit data provenance. An essential component of this approach is separating objective safety surveillance and adverse event reporting from the algorithm’s internal learning mechanisms to detect epistemic drift and automation bias. Ultimately, the successful and safe integration of intelligence-based medicine depends on an unwavering commitment to transparent governance. When computational power is harnessed as a regulated, transparent tool within an LHS, AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma, ensuring future care is anchored in dynamic, validated evidence rather than perpetuating the medical errors propagated by eminence from the past.Keywords: artificial intelligence, evidence-based medicine, intelligence-based medicine, learning health systems, medical dogma, medical epistemology 6.ConclusionThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, the dawn of intelligence-based medicine. While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care, it simultaneously introduces the risk of a modernised, digital dogma. If deployed without rigorous oversight, algorithmic systems threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics. By embedding these technologies within the continuous, self-correcting frameworks of learning health systems, separating performance surveillance from internal model learning, and aggressively auditing data provenance, we can safeguard clinical care in emergency departments. Ultimately, the successful integration of AI depends not just on computational power, but on our unwavering commitment to transparent governance, ensuring these tools actively dismantle entrenched dogma rather than perpetuating the errors of the past. 1.IntroductionMedical epistemology, the philosophical study of how medical knowledge is acquired, validated, and ultimately applied to patient care, has undergone profound transformation throughout human history (1). This evolution of clinical truth can be broadly delineated into three distinct eras (Table 1) (2). For centuries eminence-based medicine governed healthcare through deeply embedded philosophical theory, tradition, and the unquestioned authority of esteemed physicians (3). This foundational period eventually gave way to the era of evidence-based medicine, catalysed by watershed breakthroughs such as the discovery and adoption of germ theory, centring clinical care through the combination of external evidence, individual expertise and patient values and expectations (4). Today, the medical field stands at the precipice of a third revolutionary epoch: intelligence-based medicine. Defined by the deep integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into everyday care, this emerging phase shifts the locus of knowledge from static, population-level evidence to dynamic, hyper-personalised insights (5).Table 1Evolution of medical epistemology.Epistemological eraDimensionEminenceEvidenceIntelligenceIntroductionPrior to late 20th centuryLate 20th century (1990s)Early 21st century (2020s)Epistemic authorityThe Expert: Seniority, clinical intuition, historical precedence, and accumulated personal experience.The Method: Scientific empiricism, rigorous study design and statistical significance.The Algorithm: Pattern recognition, probabilistic modelling, and high-dimensional data analysisSources of knowledgeClinical lore, anecdotes, traditional texts, unstructured and expert opinionRandomised controlled trials, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and clinical guidelinesRoutinely collected data, peer reviewed, grey, professional and popular literatureStrengths at time of introductionDecisional certainty, standardised training and practisesObjective, reproducible care, patient focused, physician aligned and evaluativePersonalised care, consolidation of vast amounts of informationInherent Limits/FragilityInflexible, dogmatic, non-evaluativePopulation bias, malfeasance, labour intensiveprocess-blind, non-evaluative, automation biasDespite these paradigm shifts in medical epistemology, the underlying threat of medical dogma remains a persistent challenge across all three eras (6, 7). Medical dogma can be defined as the rigid, uncritical acceptance of clinical beliefs or practises, often maintained despite an absence of robust support or in the face of contradictory data (6, 7). This phenomenon defined the era of eminence-based medicine. While evidence-based medicine was designed to dismantle such rigid thinking, dogma continues to be a constant threat in this era. It is frequently driven by the lingering influence of eminence, which has found a powerful new vehicle in social media, where charismatic experts and rapid information sharing can entrench unverified clinical opinions as accepted truths (7, 8). Given the birth of free open access medical education by the critical care specialties, the paucity of high-quality evidence in emergency medicine and the boom of information modalities, emergency departments are particularly vulnerable (9).As we transition toward intelligence-based medicine, the risk of persistent dogmatic practise is not eliminated but potentially amplified. The opacity of AI deeply embedded within information systems can lead to an algorithmic paternalism where clinicians might unknowingly follow the advice of computational outputs, trading the unquestioned authority of historical physicians and medical influencers for the presumed infallibility of machines (10). Optimising intelligence-based medicine therefore requires transparent mechanisms to ensure it functions as an objective tool to detect and disrupt entrenched clinical dogma, rather than a silent amplifier of historical errors. Rather than requiring complete reinvention, existing learning health system frameworks can be refined to act as essential guardrails, subjecting AI inputs to rigorous governance and continuous evaluation. This approach includes systematic assessments of data provenance and real-time surveillance of data accuracy to detect epistemic drift. 2.Eminence based medicineThe epoch of eminence-based medicine represents the longest phase in the history of medical epistemology, spanning roughly from classical antiquity around 400 BCE and persisting well into the late 19th century (2). During these millennia, the foundations of medical practise were constructed not upon empirical observation, but upon sweeping, rigid philosophical frameworks (2, 11). In ancient traditions, most notably the humoral theories championed by Hippocrates, disease was fundamentally rationalised as an imbalance of elemental forces rather than a specific biological pathology (12). These early frameworks relied heavily on deductive reasoning drawn from abstract, untested principles, assuming that human physiology perfectly mirrored the macrocosm of the natural world (12).The intersection of philosophical absolutism and early medical practise cultivated a deeply authoritarian culture within the healing arts (13). Clinical hierarchies were dominated by esteemed figures whose instructions were treated as infallible doctrine (14, 15). In this environment, the hierarchy of knowledge placed the reputation, charisma, and intuition of the doctor far above the reality of the patient experience (16). The culture produced was strictly authoritarian over evidence; questioning a senior physician or challenging an established classical text was viewed as an act of professional rebellion rather than a legitimate scientific inquiry (14). An esteemed physician could rely entirely on personal anecdote and theoretical justification to mandate dangerous treatments such as trepanation, the practise of boring holes into a living patient’s skull to release trapped metaphysical humours, stagnant blood, or evil spirits to cure seizures and mental illness (14).For eminence to remain the absolute standard of truth for centuries was not only a product of professional arrogance, but because the medical community lacked technological infrastructure to support a more evidence-based approach (17, 18). The very concept of systematically evaluating treatments was slow, owing to the lack of digital capabilities (19). In an era where information was recorded manually and shared slowly across vast distances, the ability to coordinate, collect, and mathematically analyse data across multiple centres was impossible (18). 3.Evidence based medicineThe introduction of evidence-based medicine was a profound epistemological shock, demanding that clinical truth no longer be derived from ancient texts or the intuition of a master physician, but from replicable empirical data (18, 19). The breaking point for the centuries long grip of eminence-based medicine arrived not through a philosophical debate but was sparked by the undeniable visualisation of pathology and accompanying germ theory (4, 18). Championed in the 19th century by pioneers like Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch, this paradigm shift demonstrated that specific, observable microorganisms caused specific diseases, completely dismantling the abstract, unprovable tenets of humoral imbalance (12). Acceptance however was bitterly contested and painstakingly slow (1, 2, 4, 15). The early refusal to accept germ theory and empirical clinical data was deeply rooted in the preservation of professional prestige and cognitive dissonance (2). One of the more prominent historical examples was Ignaz Semmelweis who, despite demonstrating that physicians were transmitting fatal puerperal fever to mothers and mandating handwashing, was ostracised and driven out of the profession (20). The medical establishment found it deeply offensive to suggest that a gentleman’s hands could be unclean, allowing their bruised egos and entrenched dogma to completely override clear, statistical evidence of mortality reduction (20). This dogmatic persistence highlighted a critical vulnerability in the evolution of medicine that persists today, that evidence alone is insufficient to create change (6, 7).The eventual embrace of evidence-based medicine required more than just the initial visualisation of pathogens; it necessitated an entire ecosystem of new methodological and technological frameworks made available through the digital era (1, 4, 18, 19). The formalisation of randomised controlled trials, globalised data aggregation, and rapid scientific dissemination eventually catalysed and shaped the widespread acceptance of evidence-based medicine (15, 18, 19).The integrity of evidence-based medicine was not without its challenges, the greatest being scientific malfeasance (21). High-profile fraud such as Andrew Wakefield’s fabricated manuscript linking the measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine to autism, and Joachim Boldt’s extensive falsification of hydroxyethyl starch trials, demonstrate how fraudulent research can infiltrate and corrupt clinical guidelines, social expectations and compromise patient safety for decades (22–24). These breaches fundamentally destabilised the epistemic trust required for evidence-based medicine to be embraced and are still so deeply intwined that despite retractions and public discourse, remnants continue to influence care (22, 25).The shadow of eminence-based medicine also continues to linger and actively threaten clinical decision making today, paradoxically fuelled by modern digital technology (26). While evidence-based medicine relies on the slow, methodical accumulation of peer reviewed data, the architecture of social media and digital communication thrives on speed, confidence, and controversy (27, 28). Charismatic experts and social media influencers can now bypass rigorous scientific scrutiny, broadcasting anecdotal successes or theoretical opinions directly to millions of practitioners and patients instantly (27–29). In this digital environment, algorithmic amplification often elevates a compelling narrative over nuanced, statistically sound evidence (30). This creates a dangerous backdoor for eminence to reassert itself, allowing individuals to shape practise patterns based on their digital influence rather than robust clinical validation (30). As we prepare to integrate even more advanced technologies into care, we must recognise that the digital age has not eradicated medical dogma, it has merely provided it with a faster, more pervasive platform (28, 30). 4.Intelligence based medicineThe trajectory toward intelligence-based medicine represents the latest paradigm shift in clinical epistemology (5). Intelligence-based medicine transitions clinical decision making from the static, population-level approach of evidence-based medicine to dynamic computational synthesis by integrating available research, genomics, biometrics, health records, and imaging to deliver hyper-personalised guidance directly at the point of care (31). Following accelerated development of AI in the 1950s, the rapid adoption of intelligence-based care began in the earl 2020s, catalysed by the convergence of computationally affordable deep learning architectures, massive multimodal datasets, and generative AI (5, 31).While frequently conceptualised as a homogeneous entity, artificial intelligence encompasses distinct modalities with unique risk profiles and governance requirements. Rule-based clinical decision support systems execute predetermined logic to guide established protocols. In contrast, prognostic machine learning models dynamically analyse high-dimensional data to forecast outcomes. However, these models are distinctly vulnerable to subtle algorithmic drift, causing accuracy and calibration to degrade over time as patient demographics and clinical practises evolve. Generative artificial intelligence, particularly large language models, offers substantial advantages over simpler computational tools by processing and synthesising unstructured clinical narratives into cohesive insights. Despite this utility, generative models introduce profound epistemic vulnerabilities, notably the generation of factually incorrect outputs and the potentiation of automation bias. This phenomenon risks the erosion of foundational critical thinking, as clinicians facing uncertainty may uncritically defer to the machine, over relying on persuasively worded but potentially flawed computational advice.Unlike the fiercely debated shift to evidence-based medicine, the transition to intelligence-based care is advancing at an unprecedented pace, driven by the pervasive adoption of AI in everyday life (31). Because the integration of AI into clinical workflows brings significant threats alongside its transformative benefits, accelerating this paradigm shift requires robust epistemological guardrails (32). The black box nature of complex machine learning models frequently obscures the underlying logic, making verification extraordinarily difficult for bedside clinicians and patients (32, 33). This opacity risks a perilous regression to eminence-based medicine and emergence of digital dogma, wherein clinicians facing algorithmic uncertainty may uncritically defer to the machine just as classical practitioners once yielded to the unproven pronouncements of esteemed physicians and social media influencers (11, 12, 14, 29, 32). This phenomenon, known as automation bias, risks eroding foundational critical thinking and diagnostic skills, while subtle algorithmic drift can cause model accuracy to quietly degrade over time as patient demographics and clinical practises evolve and new evidence is discovered (31, 32).While artificial intelligence and algorithmic decision-support systems promise unprecedented objectivity, they are trained using highly variable datasets. Umbrella reviews assessing therapeutic interventions in emergency medicine indicate that only a marginal proportion (2.8%) of evaluated meta-analyses meet stringent criteria for high-quality evidence (34). Consequently, clinical practise frequently necessitates reliance on quasi-evidence, observational consensus, or subjective heuristics. The datasets used to train machine learning models are therefore inherently vulnerable to implicit biases, systemic inequities, and eminence-driven practise patterns (32, 33). This creates a profound epistemic risk. While retracted manuscripts exhibit distinct statistical features, they historically bypass human scrutiny to influence subsequent literature. Consequently, the capacity of an algorithm to autonomously detect and filter embedded misinformation represents a substantial functional limitation. full_text_sections.abstract: AbstractThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, intelligence-based medicine. Driven by the integration of artificial intelligence (AI), this emerging era offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care within high-stakes environments like emergency departments. However, this paradigm shift simultaneously introduces a critical risk of modernised, digital dogma, manifesting as algorithmic paternalism. If AI systems are deployed without rigorous oversight, they threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics, trading the unquestioned authority of historical figures for the presumed infallibility of machines. To safeguard care in emergency departments, AI must not operate unchecked. Adapting existing Learning Health System frameworks offers a pragmatic solution to govern AI integration. By embedding these computational technologies within continuous, self-correcting clinical ecosystems, departments can enforce robust data hygiene and rigorously audit data provenance. An essential component of this approach is separating objective safety surveillance and adverse event reporting from the algorithm’s internal learning mechanisms to detect epistemic drift and automation bias. Ultimately, the successful and safe integration of intelligence-based medicine depends on an unwavering commitment to transparent governance. When computational power is harnessed as a regulated, transparent tool within an LHS, AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma, ensuring future care is anchored in dynamic, validated evidence rather than perpetuating the medical errors propagated by eminence from the past.Keywords: artificial intelligence, evidence-based medicine, intelligence-based medicine, learning health systems, medical dogma, medical epistemology
full_text_sections.conclusion: 6.ConclusionThe evolution of medical epistemology from the unassailable authority of eminence to the empirical rigour of evidence has prepared the healthcare system for its most profound transformation yet, the dawn of intelligence-based medicine. While AI offers unprecedented capabilities to process complex health data and personalise patient care, it simultaneously introduces the risk of a modernised, digital dogma. If deployed without rigorous oversight, algorithmic systems threaten to silently amplify historical biases, diagnostic inaccuracies, and outdated clinical heuristics. By embedding these technologies within the continuous, self-correcting frameworks of learning health systems, separating performance surveillance from internal model learning, and aggressively auditing data provenance, we can safeguard clinical care in emergency departments. Ultimately, the successful integration of AI depends not just on computational power, but on our unwavering commitment to transparent governance, ensuring these tools actively dismantle entrenched dogma rather than perpetuating the errors of the past.

title_original: From eminence to evidence to intelligence-based medicine: optimising artificial intelligence to disrupt dogma in emergency departments

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the risk of modernised, digital dogma in the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into emergency departments, highlighting the need to prevent algorithmic biases and ensure clinical care remains grounded in validated evidence.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study examined the evolution of medical epistemology and the challenges of integrating AI into clinical practice, focusing on emergency departments and the broader healthcare system.
analysis.methods: The study utilised historical and contemporary examples to evaluate the risks of AI deployment, including the black box nature of machine learning models and the potential for automation bias and epistemic drift.
analysis.main_results: The findings indicate that only a marginal proportion (2.8%) of evaluated meta-analyses in emergency medicine meet stringent criteria for high-quality evidence, and that AI systems are vulnerable to implicit biases and outdated clinical heuristics.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that the integration of AI into emergency departments must be governed by transparent frameworks to prevent the emergence of digital dogma, offering a novel approach to align computational power with dynamic, validated evidence.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: These findings inform the need for rigorous oversight and governance of AI systems in emergency medicine to ensure they do not perpetuate historical biases or errors, thereby safeguarding patient care and clinical decision-making.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study relies on historical and general observations rather than specific, target-focused evidence, which limits the strength of its conclusions and necessitates further targeted research.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into emergency departments, highlighting the risks of modernised, digital dogma. It argues that AI systems, if not rigorously overseen, may amplify historical biases and diagnostic inaccuracies, undermining the principles of evidence-based medicine. The authors propose embedding AI within learning health systems to ensure transparency, continuous auditing, and separation of performance surveillance from model learning. They note that only a marginal proportion (2.8%) of evaluated meta-analyses in emergency medicine meet high-quality criteria, underscoring the need for careful governance. The study suggests that AI can actively dismantle entrenched clinical dogma if properly regulated, but its success depends on transparent frameworks that prevent algorithmic drift and automation bias. While the study provides a conceptual framework, it lacks specific, target-focused evidence, limiting its conclusions.

analysis_zh.research_question_and_background: 该研究旨在解决将人工智能 (AI) 集成到急诊科时的现代化数字教条风险,强调需要防止算法偏差并确保临床护理始终以经过验证的证据为基础。
analysis_zh.study_design_and_population: 该研究探讨了医学认识论的 进化 以及将人工智能融入临床实践的挑战,重点关注急诊科和更广泛的医疗保健系统。
analysis_zh.methods: 该研究利用历史和当代的例子来评估人工智能部署的风险,包括机器学习模型的黑匣子性质以及自动化偏差和认知漂移的可能性。
analysis_zh.main_results: 研究结果表明,在急诊医学评估的荟萃分析中,只有一小部分(2.8%)符合高质量证据的严格标准,并且人工智能系统容易受到隐性偏见和过时的临床启发法的影响。
analysis_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者解释说,人工智能与急诊部门的整合必须受到透明框架的约束,以防止数字教条的出现,从而提供一种将计算能力与动态、经过验证的证据结合起来的新颖方法。
analysis_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明需要对急诊医学中的人工智能系统进行严格的监督和治理,以确保它们不会延续历史偏见或错误,从而保障患者护理和临床决策。
analysis_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 该研究依赖于历史和一般观察,而不是具体的、以目标为中心的证据,这限制了其结论的力度,并需要进一步的有针对性的研究。

full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2356 | 2356 The enlarging scope and globalization of vaccine hesitancy By Peter Hotez As bad as it’s been, antivaccine activism is expected to worsen as it spreads from the USA to Europe and reaches into other fields of biomedicine. D uring the COVID pandemic, anti- vaccine activism became a dan- gerous and lethal force in the USA. After COVID vaccines became widely available in early 2021, what began as a reasonable public debate about immunization mandates in the work- place took a dark and dangerous turn. Parti- san media outlets introduced Americans to a range of activist contributors and pundits who falsely discredited the effectiveness and safety of mRNA vaccines. Among their false claims: mRNA vaccines would integrate into your genome and cause turbo cancers; and vaccinations were dangerous for your heart, ignoring the scientific data showing it was the SARS-CoV-2 virus inducing thromboembolic events causing heart attacks and strokes1. A vast disinformation campaign convinced hun- dreds of thousands of Americans to eschew COVID vaccines in favor of anti-parasitic drugs such as ivermectin. The consequences were deadly, with at least 200,000 unvaccinated Americans dying between mid-2021 and 2022. Health policy analyst Charles Gaba was among the first to analyze mortality data and find that deaths among unvaccinated Americans disproportionately followed a partisan divide, by a striking margin. Anti- vaccine activism became a cornerstone for ideologically driven politicians, including those tied to a wellness and influencer indus- try promoting medications or supplements of unproven benefit. Even after the human cost of vaccine refusal became clear, there was no self-reflection or course correction. The wellness industry doubled down, promoting anti-parasitic drugs as a cancer cures. In early 2025, antivaccine activism spilled over to childhood immunizations. A major measles outbreak spread from West Texas2 into neighboring states, causing dozens of hospital- izations and two deaths among unvaccinated children. In February 2025, Robert F. Kennedy Jr was sworn in as US Health Secretary, coinciding with the launch of the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) Commission. He quicklu pub- licly discredited the measles–mumps–rubella (MMR) vaccine, falsely claiming it was a “leaky” vaccine contaminated with aborted fetal rem- nants, that immunity declined by 4.5% annu- ally, and that it was linked to autism. He aligned himself with wellness influencers by endors- ing a cocktail of clarithromycin, vitamin A and budesonide, then dismissed the CDC’s Advi- sory Committee on Immunization Practices and replaced its members with less-qualified individuals. In the meantime, two further mea- sles epidemics erupted in the US Southwest and South Carolina to threaten America’s elimi- nation status. In April 2026, the US Defense Secretary ended annual flu vaccine require- ments for most service members but reversed the decision after a fatal influenza outbreak at Joint Base San Antonio-Lackland. MAHA disinformation continues to expand into new areas of biomedicine, promoting out- landish claims about fluoride in drinking water, the benefits of raw milk, the risks of electro- magnetic fields, and even the origins of Lyme disease. Autism remains a particular focus, extending beyond debunked vaccine claims to controversial statements about autistic indi- viduals and proposals for autism registries. These narratives largely ignore extensive evi- dence linking hundreds of autism-associated genes to neurodevelopment3, and their interactions with known risk factors includ- ing prenatal, valproic acid exposure4. As a pediatrician vaccine scientist, and parent of an adult a daughter with autism and intellec- tual disabilities5, I find the MAHA rhetoric and disregard for evidence deeply concerning. So where is this headed? In addition to DHHS’ ongoing efforts to dismantle US vac- cine policy built over decades, their actions attest to a greater MAHA aspiration — namely to build a parallel universe of alternative medi- cine aligned with the wellness industry. The strategy relies on undermining confidence in mainstream biomedicine while cutting or redi- recting government support for their specific projects. The 1910 Flexner Report exposed the weaknesses of sectarian medical schools teaching homeopathic and eclectic medicine, and helped drive the rise of scientific medicine and modern academic medical centres. Johns Hopkins Medical School was held up as the gold standard. That model has stood the test of time. Tragically, however, MAHA aspires to resurrect sectarianism in its new twenty-first century wellness incarnation. Another worry is the spread of MAHA pseu- doscience to Europe. Adoption of MAHA mes- saging by some politicians and media, along with the launch of a ‘Make Europe Healthy Again’ initiative, raises the possibility of a USA– EU alignment on MAHA-style health policies. As both regions face growing public health threats, including future pandemics and the ongoing Ebola epidemic, a return to ideologi- cally driven or pre-scientific approaches to medicine would be a major setback. source_body_en: Similar to other research universities, a long-standing BCM policy provides its faculty and staff, who make discoveries that result in a commercial license, a share of any royalty income. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2356 | 2356 The enlarging scope and globalization of vaccine hesitancy By Peter Hotez As bad as it’s been, antivaccine activism is expected to worsen as it spreads from the USA to Europe and reaches into other fields of biomedicine. D uring the COVID pandemic, anti- vaccine activism became a dan- gerous and lethal force in the USA. After COVID vaccines became widely available in early 2021, what began as a reasonable public debate about immunization mandates in the work- place took a dark and dangerous turn. Parti- san media outlets introduced Americans to a range of activist contributors and pundits who falsely discredited the effectiveness and safety of mRNA vaccines. Among their false claims: mRNA vaccines would integrate into your genome and cause turbo cancers; and vaccinations were dangerous for your heart, ignoring the scientific data showing it was the SARS-CoV-2 virus inducing thromboembolic events causing heart attacks and strokes1. A vast disinformation campaign convinced hun- dreds of thousands of Americans to eschew COVID vaccines in favor of anti-parasitic drugs such as ivermectin. The consequences were deadly, with at least 200,000 unvaccinated Americans dying between mid-2021 and 2022. Health policy analyst Charles Gaba was among the first to analyze mortality data and find that deaths among unvaccinated Americans disproportionately followed a partisan divide, by a striking margin. Anti- vaccine activism became a cornerstone for ideologically driven politicians, including those tied to a wellness and influencer indus- try p...

full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2363 The European Vaccines Hub Rino Rappuoli, Isabelle Bekeredjian-Ding, Pierre Van Damme, James P. Di Santo, Donata Medaglini & Michel Pletschette The European Vaccines Hub is a novel design consortium that assembles leading European organizations involved in vaccine development. The mission is to develop vaccines and monoclonal antibodies ensuring Europe’s pandemics and emerging infections readiness. When the COVID-19 pandemic struck the European Union, it was insufficiently prepared to face the devastating health and economic emergency. Although European biotech contributed significantly to the development of vaccines with products such as Comirnaty, the mRNA vaccine developed by the German BioNTech was eventually licensed to and commercialized by an American company, meaning that very few European medical countermeasures reached the market at the peak of the pandemic. A further weakness identified was that Europe did not partici- pate in any of the pivotal efficacy trials leading to licensure. To address this situation, the European Commission established the Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Authority (HERA) as one of its Directorates General, with the mission of strengthening the European Union’s ability to respond to major health threats through coordination, expertise and the development and procurement of medical countermeasures (MCMs). In the aftermath of the COVID-19 pandemic, HERA published a call for proposals for the creation of a European Hub for vaccine development, with the mission of developing, assessing and manufacturing vaccines for priority pathogens with epidemic and pandemic potential to ensure that Europe would be more resilient through increased preparedness. This new entity was designed to be not another institution, but rather a newly created network of existing organizations already funded by their member states to develop vaccines. The mandate of the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) was to create a hub able to develop and deliver vaccines end-to-end, from discovery to manufacturing. To achieve this, the EVH was expected to be organ- ized in an agile manner, allowing it to make quick decisions and to include and engage with any group from industry, biotech or academia that could contribute to development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies against pathogens with pandemic risk. Unique new structure The EVH consortium selected for funding enabled the creation of an innovative organization that has the expertise and facilities to provide the European Union with self-sustainable and independent ability to discover, develop, assess and manufacture vaccines and antibodies against infectious diseases of epidemic and pandemic potential. This organization is based on four pillars (Fig. 1). Pillar 1 leads vaccines and monoclonal antibody discovery while advancing platforms to develop vaccines based on protein and adjuvants, on mRNA or on viral vectors. Pillar 2 drives preclinical studies to support the discovery, charac- terization and development of vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. Pillar 3 coordinates clinical development, which includes the readiness to perform ad hoc phase 1 and 2 studies and controlled human challenge studies (CHIM), with the overarching goals of putting together a network of European vaccine clinical trial centers under consented protocols and preparing to conduct large-scale phase 3 studies in collaboration with the EU ‘BE READY NOW’ project. In pillar 4, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Center for Pandemic Vaccines and Therapeutics (ZEPAI) oversee regulatory coordination and planning of manufacturing of small-scale Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) lots for early clinical studies, as well as large-scale manufacturing of final products. Although the primary scope of the EVH is to develop and build the capacity to deliver medical countermeasures, it is designed as an open organization that reaches out and engages with small and large vaccine manufacturers, biotech, academic groups, R&D units of pharmaceuti- cal companies, and projects and networks funded by European Union, for example through the Horizon Europe program. To achieve this, the EVH is following two noteworthy paths: the creation of an innovative public–private partnership model with industry and the promotion of ‘expression of interest’ calls for experts and specific projects, enabling the EVH to liaise with experts and collaborating centers that share a similar mission, both within and outside the European Union. The arrows below each pillar in Fig. 1 denote the continuous interchange between the EVH and the European system. Projects Priority projects for the EVH are developments that tackle infec- tious diseases with epidemic and pandemic potential relevant to the European Union. The organization’s base is the entirety of Europe, and it is organized in four pillars that comprise the activities necessary for end-to-end vaccine delivery. The arrows below each pillar indicate that any European entity can take or bring projects. CHIM, controlled human challenge studies. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2364 Comment with HERA. The initial priority pathogens identified were avian influ- enza, in particular H5N1, and monkeypox (mpox). EVH activities include building the preparedness system and testing it. Indeed, the EVH’s mission creates a system that allows continuous delivery and regular updates for priorities. A living EU Epidemic and Pandemic Vaccine Readiness Plan agreed to with HERA generates an agile basis for EU pandemic preparedness. One year after the EVH was established, each of the four pillars has initiated a variety of projects and delivered important results. Pillar 1 discovered a potent and broadly protective monoclonal anti- body against mpox that recognizes a vaccine antigen not previously known to induce neutralizing antibodies. In vivo and in vitro studies in collaboration with pillar 2 confirmed that the mpox monoclonal antibody and the vaccine antigen are protective in vivo and are good candidates for continued MCM development. Pillar 3 has designed and fully enrolled a clinical trial to study the vaccine response of the European population to primary and booster immunization against the avian influenza H5N1, and is currently assessing its outcome. In the trial, H5N1-naive participants and participants immunized in 2006 with a H5N1 vaccine received an adjuvanted vaccine against the current Astrakhan clade. The study has the additional scope to establish a study cohort whose peripheral blood cells can be used to discover broadly neutralizing antibodies that recognize epitopes shared between the 2006 and 2026 H5N1 strains. Pillar 4 is addressing important bottlenecks in preparedness by mapping the European GMP facilities ready to manufacture vaccines and monoclonals for small-scale clinical trials and developing concepts for rapid ramp-up to large-scale manufacturing in pandemic crises. Its regulatory experts are addressing the anticipated practical and scientific regulatory questions required for accelerating development of EVH products to enable early availability of products. In addition, the EVH has initiated collaborations with external entities. One involves joint participation with Sanofi, a major Euro- pean vaccine manufacturer, in an EU tender to develop a mucosal mRNA vaccine against the H5N1 avian influenza. Another involves the publication of an ‘expression of interest’ to identify possible col- laborators that can contribute to further pandemic influenza vaccine development approaches. Stress testing While the EVH was working on setting up its organization, two unex- pected, highly lethal emerging infections were communicated by the World Health Organization in May 2026. The first was the Andes hanta- virus outbreak, reported on 2 May, involving a cruise ship coming out of Argentina1, and the second was the Ebola Bundibugyo outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Uganda that was declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern on 17 May2. Although these were not imminent threats for Europe, after rapid consultation with HERA, it was agreed that it would be important for Europe to par- ticipate in the development of countermeasures for these viruses. The question was whether the EVH had the capacity to address these two targets that, up to that moment, had never been considered. Consultation of the EVH network identified a broadly protective human monoclonal antibody against Andes hantavirus discovered in a Swedish patient infected with Puumala hantavirus, which had been characterized by several German academic groups and whose structure had been determined a few years ago at the Institut Pasteur in Paris3. This antibody had been acquired and improved by two US R&D enterprises but was never brought into clinical development. Concurrently, the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) labora- tories revealed recent results identifying a potent human monoclonal antibody that neutralizes both Ebola Zaire and Ebola Bundibugyo. The antibody had been shown to protect mice from challenge with the virus in the Biosafety Level 4 (BSL4) facility in Marburg4. As such, in less than a month, the two antibodies were selected by the EVH for development up to clinical testing. For antibody expression, EVH is developing an innovative platform based on the C1 fungus, which is expected to enable cost-effective production of large quantities of monoclonal antibodies, making these therapies more accessible to at-risk populations and to low-income countries at an affordable and equitable cost5. The stress test arising from the unexpected outbreaks showed that the EVH can leverage the ad hoc development of a multitude of innova- tive prototypes from excellent European entities that have hitherto failed to translate them into products when working in isolation. The EVH can turn these product candidates into countermeasures to protect people’s health. Moreover, the EVH network had at its disposal two vac- cine prototypes for the development of an Ebola vaccine: an MVA-based vaccine against Ebola Zaire developed by DZIF-associated EVH mem- bers, previously shown to be protective in a mouse challenge study performed at the Marburg BSL-4 facility6, and a measles vector-based pan-filovirus vaccine in development at the Institut Pasteur. Once added to the EVH portfolio, these projects could become highly relevant in the race against Bundibugyo virus. Furthermore, monoclonal antibodies candidates could provide an important complementary strategy, with the advantage of providing immediate protection. Looking to the future In conclusion, the EVH is an organization rooting pandemic prepar- edness within an innovative cross-sectorial ecosystem, which in its first year of existence has shown the potential to deliver innovative countermeasures. We can probably describe the EVH as both a dis- covery and development engine and a catalyst able to aggregate the best European competencies and discoveries, transforming them into medical products that include vaccines and monoclonal antibodies. The big question is whether the EVH will be able to exploit this poten- tial and deliver real products. There are numerous challenges that could interfere with this ambitious goal. One of the most important limitations is the fact that the products in the EVH portfolio do not have an immediate attractive commercial market value because they address infectious diseases that are rare, or pandemics that we hope will never happen. The absence of immediate commercial value, com- monly defined as a market failure, is a recurrent problem for most medical countermeasures. In the absence of an expected immediate and secure return on investment, the private sector is little inclined to start rapid development and manufacturing programs. Notwithstand- ing that complication, the instruments developed by the EU in terms of stockpiling essential and possibly innovative MCMs and the constant readiness of the reality-tested joint procurement mechanism are robust attempts to provide solutions to these problems. Although we have the technology to develop effective products against most infectious diseases, these need to become available for wide implementation despite the absence of immediate pre- dictable markets. It is therefore important to address, on a global scale, the longer-term sustainability of MCM development, which can be clearly seen to be an insurance for the health and economic security of every country, and to move out of the disastrous cycle of panic and neglect. nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2363–2365 | 2365 Comment Rino Rappuoli 1,2 , Isabelle Bekeredjian-Ding1,3,4, Pierre Van Damme 1,5, James P. full_text: nature immunology Volume 27 | December 2026 | 2355 | 2355 Vaccinology 2.0 The COVID-19 pandemic highlighted the success of vaccine development, but more improvements in vaccine design, equity, manufacturing and changes in public health policy are warranted. O ne of the global health success stories has been the develop­ ment of vaccines. According to the World Health Organization (WHO), we now have vaccines to more than 30 life-threatening infections, which is estimated to prevent 3.5 million to 5 million deaths every year. The recent COVID-19 pandemic showcased vaccine development at its best. Vaccines against SARS-CoV-2 were developed at record speed, facilitated by new technologies such as the mRNA vaccine platform and spurred by the wealth of existing knowledge of virology, vac­ cinology and structural biology. However, much has changed since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. In this issue of Nature Immunology, we have commissioned several commentaries from experts across the globe that collectively summarize recent progress and discuss the challenges faced in this field. Although the COVID-19 pandemic high­ lighted the transformative potential of mRNA platforms, gaps remain for global pandemic preparedness according to Florian Kram­ mer. In his Comment, Krammer argues that there is a need to advance mucosal vaccines to improve protection against respiratory infection and transmission, and to develop more broadly protective vaccines that target entire virus families. In addition, strengthen­ ing regulatory policy and sustaining support for basic research on emerging pathogens is needed. However, the current US adminis­ tration has adopted measures that weaken vaccine development in the USA by the deci­ sion to withdraw federal support for mRNA vaccine development. This action led to the cancellation of research grant contracts worth approximately US$500 million, affecting ongoing mRNA therapeutic projects involv­ ing universities, research institutes and major pharmaceutical companies. In addition to funding cuts, the public health policies of the current US government are promoting vaccine hesitancy. In a World View article, Peter Hotez argues that the rise of the US Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has weakened confidence in evidence-based medicine, contributed to out­ breaks of vaccine-preventable diseases such as measles, and fostered efforts to replace established scientific and regulatory frame­ works with wellness-oriented ideologies. Wor­ ryingly, vaccine hesitancy has evolved from a movement focused on COVID-19 vaccines into a broader anti-science campaign that increas­ ingly shapes public health policy, promotes misinformation and extends to areas such as childhood immunization, autism, fluoride, raw milk and alternative medicine. Further­ more, Hotez warns that these trends are spreading internationally, particularly into Europe, raising concerns that growing accept­ ance of pseudoscientific health policies could undermine pandemic preparedness, biomedi­ cal research and public health outcomes on a global scale. On a more optimistic note, in their Com­ ment Michael J. Hogan and Norbert Pardi discuss advances across other RNA technolo­ gies that aim to improve efficacy, reduce reac­ togenicity and enhance T cell and mucosal immune responses. A deeper understanding of RNA and lipid-nanoparticle biology, com­ bined with innovations in delivery systems and immune modulation, is still needed to engi­ neer vaccines that produce different types of immune response depending on the disease being treated. Similarly, the COVID-19 pan­ demic exposed the vulnerability of Africa and other lower-income regions to dependence on external vaccine suppliers. Shabir A. Madhi and Glenda E. Gray state in their Comment that the local manufacturing of routine vaccines in Africa is often economically uncompeti­ tive and may divert resources from broader public health goals. Instead, they advocate for strategic investment in adaptable vaccine platforms such as mRNA and viral-vector technologies, outbreak-response manufac­ turing capacity, regulatory expertise, clini­ cal development infrastructure and skilled workforce development. In their Comment, Rino Rappuoli et al. high­ light the European Vaccines Hub for Pandemic Readiness (EVH) created in response to short­ comings exposed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The EVH is designed to strengthen pandemic preparedness by integrating vaccine and monoclonal antibody discovery, preclinical and clinical development, regulatory plan­ ning and manufacturing capabilities into a coordinated, end-to-end development net­ work. The initiative aims to translate Europe’s strong scientific base into deployable medi­ cal countermeasures for emerging infectious diseases and is currently focusing on threats such as H5N1 influenza. The authors highlight EVH’s early achievements, including the iden­ tification of promising vaccine and antibody candidates, the establishment of clinical trial infrastructure, and rapid responses to emerging threats, such as Andes hantavirus and Ebola Bundibugyo outbreaks. Finally, in his Comment, Bali Pulendran looks at the future of vaccine research by pointing out the vaccine-induced protection extends beyond antibody and T cell responses to encompass a broader spectrum of ‘protec­ tive immune states’ within tissues, in which coordinated networks of immune and non­ immune cells confer heightened resistance to infection. Recent studies of intravenous BCG and mucosal vaccination suggest that protection can emerge from coordinated interactions among adaptive immune cells, innate cells and structural cells within tissues. These interactions create organ-embedded states of increased resistance that provide broad protection against diverse pathogens, a phenomenon termed ‘integrated organ immu­ nity’. Pulendran proposes that future vacci­ nology should shift from focusing primarily on antigens and immune correlates toward identifying, characterizing and deliberately engineering these protective immune states, potentially enabling more durable and broadly protective vaccines against infectious diseases and other immune-mediated conditions. This ‘Vaccinology 2.0’ focus highlights the achievements of vaccine research in the past 6 years and showcases issues that still need to be tackled to ensure the continued development, improvement and accessibility of vaccines for future generations and ensure that we are prepared for the next pandemic.
